articles.title: Florida gov. candidate Byron Donalds responds after Trump mentions removed from site
articles.summary: Some prominent references to President Trump were scrubbed from Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds' campaign website in recent weeks, but the Repu...
articles.body:
Some prominent references to President Trump were scrubbed from Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds' campaign website in recent weeks — but the Republican said Wednesday he isn't backing away from the president's agenda.

During an onstage interview at the Sunshine Economy Summit, Donalds said his campaign has "been working on website changes for, like, two months now." He said the changes are meant to reinforce the campaign's key policy themes ahead of the general election, including affordability.

"These are the issues we talk about every day on the campaign trail," he told Tom Hudson of public media organization WLRN. "For the general election, the voters of Florida want to know the policies you're going to implement to make their lives better. And so, we wanted to make sure that the website fully reflected the vision and the policies for the future of Florida."

Asked whether the changes suggest that he no longer intends to "enact the Trump agenda," a phrase that his campaign site previously listed as one of its top issues, Donalds said: "No, I think that's a separate question."

Donalds called the president's agenda a "common-sense agenda" that is "centered around law and order, sound markets, making sure that we secure our nation's borders, making sure that we continue to work with the federal government when it comes to immigration policy."

The summit, which was hosted by the Greater Fort Lauderdale Alliance, also featured an interview with Donalds' opponent, Democratic nominee David Jolly.

Previously, Donalds' status as a staunch Trump ally was difficult to miss. The homepage of his campaign website noted several times that Donalds was endorsed by Mr. Trump, and it featured a photo of the president and the congressman giving thumbs-up signs to the camera, according to an archived version of the site from earlier this month. The site's "Issues" page was also topped by a promise to "Enact the Trump Agenda."

Now, Donalds' nod from the president still appears on a scrolling list of endorsements from conservative figures, and his role as a 2024 Trump campaign surrogate is mentioned, but the president's name does not appear as extensively. The "Issues" page also no longer names the president, instead leading with the slogan: "Accountable, Achievable, Affordable!"

The changes, first reported by the Miami Herald on Tuesday, drew nationwide attention and generated speculation about whether Donalds is seeking to keep the president at arm's length.

Donalds has closely aligned himself with the president for years. Ahead of the 2024 race, he endorsed Mr. Trump over Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in the GOP primary.

Mr. Trump endorsed Donalds last year, shortly before he formally launched his campaign .

"Byron Donalds would be a truly Great and Powerful Governor for Florida and, should he decide to run, will have my Complete and Total Endorsement," Mr. Trump said. "RUN, BYRON, RUN!"

articles.title: Judge orders White House to restore access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico
articles.summary: A federal judge ordered early Thursday that the White House immediately restore access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, saying that President Donald Trump’s directive barring the three news outlets was most likely unconstitutional.
articles.body: A federal judge ordered early Thursday that the White House immediately restore access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, saying that President Donald Trump’s directive barring the three news outlets was most likely unconstitutional. In granting a 14-day temporary restraining order reinstating the outlets’ access while their legal challenge proceeds, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their lawsuit against the Trump administration, at least on the grounds that their credentials were revoked last week without due process. Trump, he wrote, did not dispute that the outlets “did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for overnight comment from NBC News. “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action,” the attorney representing the news outlets, Ted Boutrous, said in a statement. Trump had posted on social media before a Wednesday hearing in the case that he expected the “totally disloyal” Kelly, whom he nominated to the bench during his first term, to rule against him — adding that “as usual, we’ll go for appeal.” Trump announced the ban on the three news outlets in a post on Truth Social on Friday, saying it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he said. Thursday’s order rejected the White House’s argument that banning the outlets was motivated by national security concerns, saying it offered little proof to back up the claim. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office a short time after the post, Trump referred to his directive as “the ban on the free press.” “I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said. He said the policy was not in response to a particular report, but because of “cumulative stories over the last few years.” “They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added. The outlets said in their suit challenging the ban that Trump’s remarks show the policy was motivated by “retaliation” and “intended to cow” the outlets “into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate.” The “Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on that official’s dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is patently unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they argued. The White House appeared to be trying to address those due process claims in letters to the news outlets on Tuesday, which told them they could “contest this initial decision” in written responses by Friday. The letters accuse them of publishing “sensitive security information, and misinformation” which “undermines the President’s ability to safeguard the national security.” They cited specific articles about munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia, but also one about a request for $1 billion in funding for East Wing renovations that the president had said would be fully funded by donors, and another about negative “vibes” at the recent Republican midterm convention. Addressing the “extraordinary” standard that the government argued gave it the right to revoke the outlets’ passes without prior notice, Kelly wrote that the sorts of stories cited in the letters “are routine,” and stretch back months or even years. The letters also allege the organizations have “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex.” Trump made a similar argument in a Truth Social post Monday. “It is called the Oval Office, and it should be treated with Decorum, Respect, and Dignity, not defiled by Third Rate Clowns, who purposefully distort, twist, and degrade with everything they write or publish,” he wrote. But Kelly pointed to a D.C. Circuit Court case, also involving Trump, that found that for a reporter’s hard pass to be revoked, the government must first publish standards of conduct that would lead to the revocation. Nothing in the record demonstrates “formally articulated standards,” the judge wrote. And one standard the defendants “appear to offer” — reflected in the letters sent to the outlets — “is so vague it hardly does the trick.” NBC News previously reported that Trump’s Friday announcement caught a number of high-level White House aides off guard. A senior White House official defended the move to NBC News earlier this week, saying, “Nobody close to the President was surprised at his action to hold the fake news accountable.” The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents’ Association and a group of 49 news and media organizations — including NBCUniversal Media LLC, the parent company of NBC News — filed a legal brief in the case Wednesday backing the three outlets. The filing said the president’s stated reasons for the ban “are transparently viewpoint discriminatory” and “inconsistent with the First Amendment.” “The ban at issue in this case does exactly what longstanding D.C. Circuit precedent” has said the government can’t do, the filing said — “prohibited three news organizations from access to the entirety of the White House and its grounds due to the content of their reporting.” It also clashes, the filing said, “with bedrock Supreme Court precedent, which recognizes that ‘even though a person has no ‘right’ to a valuable governmental benefit,’ the government ‘may not deny a benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected interests — especially, his interest in freedom of speech.’”

articles.title: Judge orders White House to immediately restore access to CNN, MS NOW, Politico
articles.summary: A federal judge ordered the White House early Thursday to immediately restore press credentials for reporters at CNN, MS NOW and Politico, ruling that President Trump’s ban likely violated their constitutional due process rights. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly handed down the ruling in the middle of the night, hours after holding an emergency hearing on the outlets’ lawsuit. …
articles.body:
A federal judge ordered the White House early Thursday to immediately restore press credentials for reporters at CNN, MS NOW and Politico, ruling that President Trump’s ban likely violated their constitutional due process rights. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly handed down the ruling in the middle of the night, hours after holding an emergency hearing on the outlets’ lawsuit. His ruling lasts for two weeks. The trio of outlets sued after being denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday. The administration sent letters to the outlets pointing to national security concerns, but those weren’t sent until afterward. “Defendants do not dispute that Plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked,” wrote Kelly, a Trump appointee. It’s a similar rationale to the one the judge issued in 2018, when then-CNN White House reporter Jim Acosta’s hard pass was revoked. In both, the judge found that he’s bound by a 1977 decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that the Fifth Amendment’s procedural due process protections kick in when the White House arbitrarily denies a press credential to reporters. The Trump administration had told the judge the decision should be overturned. “Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” Kelly wrote. Ahead of the ruling, Trump had predicted he would lose and already vowed to appeal. “This is a judge who’s not a particularly fair judge,” the president said earlier this week. In court, the administration has defended banning the trio of news organizations by pointing to national security concerns, singling out specific stories the outlets wrote. The president deflected on Tuesday when asked whether he would restore access for CNN, Politico and MS NOW if the judge ordered it. “I think we have a right to clean out fake news,” Trump said.

articles.title: Judge temporarily overturns Trump's White House media ban
articles.summary: A court has ordered the US government to reinstate access to the building for CNN, Politico and MS NOW.
articles.body:
A judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate access to the White House for three news organisations barred from the building last week by the president.

A District of Columbia court issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, meaning CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored for 14 days, after ruling the move "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".

The three outlets launched a legal challenge after their reporters had their passes for the White House confiscated and were denied access.

The Trump administration defended the move in court, accusing the outlets of publishing false information and threatening national security - an argument the court rejected.

The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action.

Judge Timothy Kelly ruled CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in implementing the ban.

He also cast doubt on the Trump administration's arguments that the bans were motivated by national security concerns, pointing out the president made no mention of that in his initial announcement.

When President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, he accused the three news outlets of writing "fake news" and "fictions and lies" in their coverage of him and his team.

The ruling continued: "The record lacks factual support for Defendants' contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds."

In its defence of the ban in a court filing on Tuesday, the Trump administration cited a number of articles published by the outlets, including some about construction at the White House, including work on a new ballroom.

The judge said that "in most cases" the stories the White House took issue with were written by journalists who "did not even hold card passes" - and in the remaining cases, the Trump administration did not demonstrate "reason to believe that the reporter's possession of the hard pass was integral to the stories identified".

In its original filing, the Trump administration cited declarations from defence department officials supporting the ban - but the judge said they had "no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House, or about any of the facts at issue here".

Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, told CNN : "This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law."

On Monday, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties in protest at the ban. The arrangement sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.

Forty-nine media organisations - including CBS News, The New York Times and Fox News - also filed a legal brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico's lawsuit.

Trump frequently criticises news organisations, and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.

Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

articles.title: Trump-Xi summit: Here’s what’s on the agenda, and why it matters
articles.summary: The leaders of the US and China are expected to discuss trade, AI and Iran in their third in-person meeting in a year.
articles.body:
China’s leader Xi Jinping is expected to hold highly anticipated talks with United States President Donald Trump in Washington on Thursday, as both sides seek to ease trade tensions and discuss increasingly capable artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

On Wednesday evening, Trump and US First Lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, with a rare red carpet welcome. No US president had previously welcomed a visiting guest personally at the base in six decades.

Earlier in the day, China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported that Xi and Peng were being accompanied by the president’s closest aide and adviser, Cai Qi, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

The White House said the talks scheduled for Thursday would mark “a significant milestone in the relationship between the two countries”.

But the state visit – Xi’s first to the US in more than a decade – is likely to touch on multiple points of tension, including the US-Israel war on Iran, the fallout from Trump’s tariffs and the threat of war over the island of Taiwan, which China claims as its territory.

Trump met Xi on his arrival at Joint Base Andrews. But the main event is on Thursday morning, when Xi will receive a ceremonial welcome at the White House, accompanied by a military flyover and nearly 500 military personnel.

After the two leaders hold talks during the day, Trump will host a state dinner for Xi at the White House. This event is expected to include chiefs of companies important in both markets, such as Apple’s Tim Cook, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

The visit will wrap up on Friday morning when the two presidential couples will have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives to round off the trip.

Instead ⁠of a joint news conference or statement at the end, the countries are expected to issue separate announcements highlighting what each side hopes to convey to its own domestic audience.

Before the main meeting on Thursday, the two sides have already walked away from an imminent cliff: their current 11-month trade truce was set to expire in November, but has now been extended until January 10, giving their negotiating teams more time to hammer out a broader deal.

The US-Israel war on Iran is also likely to ⁠feature prominently in the discussions. Beijing has maintained close ties with Tehran, but it is unclear whether a meeting with Xi will do anything to help Trump break the ongoing deadlock in the conflict. Washington may hope that Beijing could use its influence over Tehran, observers say, but Trump has so far maintained he sees no need to seek China’s help.

The two countries are also likely to talk more about the race to develop AI, as they are in fierce competition but mindful of growing dangers. The US has proposed a new “notification mechanism” with China to alert each other of any AI incident serious enough to threaten national security.

China is also expected to raise the issue of Taiwan. In December, the Trump administration approved an $11bn arms sale to Taiwan, the largest ever, but a second package, worth some $14bn, has been on hold for months. Trump has described the arms sales as a “very good negotiating chip”.

Trump is also expected to seek the release of some Americans and others imprisoned in China, after securing the July release of Pastor Ezra Jin , a Chinese national jailed as part of the 2025 crackdown on underground churches in China. Trump had raised the pastor’s case with Xi in May.

What are relations between Trump and Xi like?

Trump’s decision to greet Xi personally upon arrival shows how far the US president is going to honour China’s leader, observers say. During a TV interview, Melania Trump said her husband had decided to greet Xi because they “have a great relationship”.

“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said of Xi and his wife during the interview with Fox News.

Despite the conciliatory tones, however, the two leaders’ ties have been strained by a trade war that began shortly after Trump returned to office for a second presidential term in January 2025.

The US president imposed a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods over fentanyl and immigration concerns, while China responded with levies on US coal, liquefied natural gas (LNG), crude oil and autos, and curbs on exports of five rare-earth metals that are essential for the manufacture of defence equipment and clean energy.

Both sides escalated rapidly, with tariffs reaching triple digits and Beijing also warning its citizens against US travel. China also threatened to impose curbs on the export of seven more rare-earth metals late last year.

That was put on hold when Trump and Xi struck a trade truce following talks in South Korea in October 2025. When the US president travelled to China in May this year, they announced plans to create a Board of Trade and Investment, ⁠while Xi agreed to purchases of Boeing jets and US farm products.

But Trump has since imposed new 12.5 percent tariffs on goods from 60 trading partners, including China, over allegations that those countries failed to curb imports made ⁠by forced labour.

Thursday’s meeting at the White House marks the two leaders’ third in-person meeting in a little less than a year amid what has been described as a reprieve in hostilities.

Both sides continue to test one another while avoiding an escalation. During Trump’s state visit, the two sides agreed to “a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, a diplomatic framework often referred to as “constructive strategic stability”.

The meeting will prove a further test of whether such a posture can hold in light of each side’s competing interests.

This balancing act could yield deals to reduce tariffs in specific sectors, cooperate on drug trafficking, and expand military-to-military dialogue.

It could also set the course for steady, long-term development of bilateral relations and confirm cooperation as the mainstay.

articles.title: US judge blocks Trump’s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico
articles.summary: Trump-nominated judge rules that outlets are likely to succeed in claim they were denied due process.
articles.body:
A United States judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s ban on three news outlets from the White House, ordering his administration to immediately restore their access pending a later court hearing.

Issuing a temporary restraining order early on Thursday, US District Judge Timothy J Kelly said CNN, MS NOW and Politico were likely to prevail in their legal challenge to Trump’s ban on several grounds, including that it violated their due process rights.

Kelly said the outlets had made a convincing case that they were stripped of their credentials without due process and were likely to suffer “irreparable harm” in the absence of the temporary order.

Kelly, who was nominated by Trump during his first term in 2017, also found there was a public interest in blocking the ban “given the importance of the free press”.

Rejecting the Trump administration’s claim that the outlets had been barred to protect national security, Kelly said the government’s argument lacked “factual support”.

“Defendants offer no declarations or other support – classified or unclassified – explaining how any of the reporting they identified in their letters to Plaintiffs damaged the national security,” Kelly said in the ruling.

Kelly ruled that the Trump administration should “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the outlets’ access to the White House.

Kelly imposed the injunction for 14 days, pending further proceedings.

Theodore Boutrous, the lawyer representing the outlets, welcomed the ruling as a vindication of the “freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law”.

“We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action,” Boutrous said in a statement.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump, who has launched a slew of attacks on the media as president, on Friday announced that he had barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from covering the White House, citing their reporting of unspecified “fake news”.

Trump later claimed in a news conference that the outlets produced “negative news” and sought to “diminish” his administration and the Republican Party.

CNN, Politico and MS NOW on Monday announced they had jointly filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn the ban, arguing it violated their free speech and due process rights.

articles.title: Republicans face brutal midterm headwinds. Six forces could help them defy history.
articles.summary: With six weeks until Election Day, rising gas prices, Trump's 39% approval rating and redistricting wars will shape the 2026 midterm battle.
articles.body: With six weeks to go until Election Day and early voting already underway in a handful of states, the conventional wisdom is that Republicans may be in for some setbacks in the midterms. As it defends its fragile House and Senate majorities, the GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the president's party lose congressional seats during the midterms. It's also battling high costs at the grocery stores and gas pumps tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, as well as President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings. But Democrats are saddled with their own issues, from an ideological civil war between the party's left wing and the establishment that has handed Republicans plenty of political ammunition, to a brand image that's nothing to brag about. Add to that the Democrats' major disadvantage as the GOP floods the airwaves with attack ads. Here are six forces that will likely determine whether Republicans can turn back a possible blue wave and hold power in Congress. WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM ELECTION POLLING 1. Inflation Six weeks until Election Day, and just as the voting begins, fuel prices keep rising, with the national average for gas nearly $4.50 per gallon and diesel topping $6.50 per gallon, according to AAA. Public opinion polls point to the economy, including the cost of living, as the top issue for voters in this year's midterms. That means that the issue that boosted Trump and Republicans to sweeping victories in 2024 is a major liability in 2026. And the rising prices in recent weeks, fueled by renewed fighting in the war with Iran and Ukraine and attacks on Russia's diesel industry, are doing the GOP no favors. "Gas prices were much higher under Biden than under ‘TRUMP.’ So were almost all other prices," the president argued Monday in a social media post, as he referred to former President Joe Biden. While Trump and Republican leaders point fingers at Biden, polls indicate voters increasingly place the blame for ongoing economic and inflation pressures on the current administration. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Democrats last week heavily criticized Trump and Republicans after the president argued that fuel costs were "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done," as he pointed to the attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities. Meanwhile, the latest Fox News poll indicated that by a wide margin, the Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation. But when asked about the overall economy, recent national surveys from Reuters/Ipsos and NBC News had the GOP and Democrats all knotted up on which party would better handle the issue. "My listeners are looking for prices to come down across the board," New Hampshire-based center-right talk radio host Jack Heath told Fox News Digital. "People elected President Trump to lower prices and improve their situation and people are looking for that improvement," Heath, host of "Good Morning NH," emphasized. "They're looking for Trump to deliver on his promises." 2. Trump's influence "I'm asking you to just pretend I'm on the ballot just one more time," the president said last week during a campaign stop in battleground North Carolina. It's a line Trump repeatedly used earlier this month, at the GOP's first-ever midterm convention. Facing what polls indicate is an enthusiasm gap with Democrats, the president and Republican leaders are hoping to energize the MAGA base, which doesn't always vote when Trump isn't on the ballot. While the president's approval rating in the Fox News poll stands at 39% among all voters, it remains at a sky-high 98% among self-described MAGA Republicans. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But some longtime Trump allies are starting to break with the president as they face challenging re-elections. GOP Rep. Maria Salazar won re-election two years ago by 20 points in South Florida's 27th Congressional District. But with Trump's negative poll numbers a potential anchor around her, Salazar last week released a TV ad criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement as having "gone too far," and that "Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today." Meanwhile, on Monday, two Trump allies who are in heated Senate battles — Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa and former Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan, broke with the president as they demanded a swift end to the war with Iran. Watch whether vulnerable Republicans create more distance from the president, or move toward Trump to juice Republican turnout. 3. Democrats' Leftward Lurch Republicans are aiming to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election, as they spotlight major Democratic primary victories this year by far-left and socialist candidates over more mainstream Democrats. "In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually, they’re communists," Trump charged at the midterm convention. The messaging is pronounced in Michigan's crucial Senate race, where GOP nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers, as he referred to Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, told FOX Business this week, "We don’t want this socialism nonsense in our state, and this guy is too extreme." 12 SENATE RACES THAT WILL DETERMINE WHO CONTROLS THE CHAMBER Polling gives a boost to the GOP's "commonsense vs. crazy" messaging. Fifty-five percent of registered voters surveyed in the latest Fox News national poll held an unfavorable view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), while only three in 10 saw the DSA in a positive light. The Fox News poll was the latest national survey to show that while the DSA has gained traction among Democrats, the group and the broader socialist movement in America face significant national skepticism. While the GOP full court press continues, in hopes of swaying undecided voters, Democrats are divided on its effectiveness. Ty Strong, founder and president of the Moderate PAC, warned that the GOP playbook "absolutely could be effective." But Shannon Jackson, a key consultant and advisor to progressive leader Rep. Ro Khanna of California, argued that Republicans are "reaching for things. I think the DSA issue is something they’re trying to make something, but it is not." Meanwhile, this year's primary surge by socialist and left-wing candidates isn't helping Democrats boost their brand. The party's favorable ratings hit historic lows in the months following the 2024 election, and the latest Fox News poll indicates Democrats are still well underwater, with 55% of voters viewing the party in an unfavorable light. 4. GOP's Money Bomb Republicans enjoy a formidable cash advantage over the Democrats, and they're using it in the final stretch leading up to Election Day. While Democratic candidates in many key races have outraised their GOP opponents, the Republican National Committee remains far ahead of the rival Democratic National Committee when it comes to cash-on-hand. And GOP-aligned outside groups, including the Trump-allied MAGA Inc., are opening the floodgates when it comes to ad spending, in order to try and level the playing field by overcoming the difficult political environment. Republican groups have outspent their Democratic counterparts by more than $83 million to run spots in ten crucial Senate races since the start of September, according to figures from AdImpact, a nationally known firm that tracks ad spending. While a financial advantage is not always decisive, strategists say it can often move the needle in a close contest. And in the 10 Senate races spotlighted by AdImpact, a onetime Democratic ad spending advantage over the summer turned into a major GOP deluge. While much of the ad dollars dished out by Republicans are to protect vulnerable seats, the money may help as the GOP works to flip open-Democrat-held Senate seats in Michigan and New Hampshire. 5. Redistricting Wars Thirteen months ago, Texas passed a new congressional redistricting map, giving Trump his first major victory in his push to give Republicans a big boost heading into the midterm elections by drawing more right-leaning districts. Fast-forward to present day, and as they fight to hold their razor-thin House majority, Republicans were the big winners, with partisan redistricting netting them potentially 10 additional right-leaning congressional seats in time for the midterms. But redrawing the maps and winning the seats are two different things, and some election analysts caution that the fierce headwinds facing the GOP could lead to Republicans falling far short of their original expectations heading into the redistricting wars. 6. House Field Narrows, Senate Map Broadens There are 435 seats in the House of Representatives, but the Cook Report suggests the battle for the chamber's majority could come down to just 21 districts it rates as a toss-up. The Fox News Power Rankings list 17 seats as true toss-ups. Decades of gerrymander, including this cycle's mid-decade redistricting, have made a major impact by narrowing the House battlefield, which may limit the number of pickups by the Democrats even if a blue wave forms. While the number of competitive House seats stays historically small, the Senate map is widening, which is a positive sign for Democrats. Democrats are feeling the heat in open-seat contests in Michigan and New Hampshire, two must-holds for them as they try to win back a Senate currently controlled 53-47 by the GOP. But Senate showdowns in red states, including Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa, are now considered very competitive. But recent polling is also giving Republicans hope they can flip the Democrat-controlled open Senate seat in blue-leaning Minnesota.

articles.title: MN Dem Sen candidate in hot seat over upcoming event hosted by man enveloped in fraud scandal: 'Red flags'
articles.summary: Peggy Flanagan's fundraiser is co-hosted by Minnesota's Medicaid Medical Director Nathan Chomilo, who served during the massive fraud scandal.
articles.body: Minnesota Lt. Gov. and Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan is set to attend a fundraiser hosted by an individual who has served as the state’s Medicaid medical director during a time period where Medicaid fraud exploded onto the national scene. Dr. Nathan Chomilo has served as Minnesota’s Medicaid medical director since January 2020 and is listed as one of the hosts of an October 1 fundraiser supporting Flanagan, first reported by Townhall’s Dustin Grage. Much of Minnesota’s broader fraud scandal has centered on Medicaid-funded programs, including autism services and Housing Stabilization Services, and although Chomilo was not the official responsible for processing payments, investigating fraud or overseeing the department’s program-integrity operations, the optics of Flanagan associating with him is sparking skepticism about Flanagan's commitment to tackling the fraud issue. "Apparently, the people who were supposed to be watching the money are too busy raising it for Peggy Flanagan," Grage posted on X. "This should raise some serious red flags." 'WE HAVE NOT SLOWED DOWN': MINNESOTA NOT OUT OF THE WOODS ON MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL, EXPERT WARNS "Things that make you go hmm… ," Chuck Darrell, former communications director at Minnesota Family Council posted on X. "The number one thing going on with Minnesota's Medicaid program has been fraud over the last eight years of the Walz Flanagan administration," Minnesota Republican State Rep. Kristin Robbins told Fox News Digital. "So he must have been aware. He must have known and clearly he had oversight responsibilities. He probably should have been held accountable for what was going on in the program and instead he's raising money for Penny Peggy Flanigan." "It just shows her disdain for the taxpayers," Robbins, the chair of the last legislative session’s Fraud Prevention and State Agency Oversight Policy Committee, continued, adding that Flanagan has "shown time and again disdain for Minnesotans who aren't on board with her radical agenda and this is just another example of that." MN DEM SENATE CANDIDATE'S VIRAL HIJAB VIDEO TAKES NEW TURN AS WOMAN BESIDE HER FACES MAJOR STATE INVESTIGATION Chomilo was highlighted in an online profile in 2023, as warning signs were surfacing about potential Medicaid fraud in the state, as a healthcare professional who was focused on "incorporating community collaboration and racial equity into Minnesota’s Medicaid policy development." "Communities experiencing inequities in health and opportunity due to structural racism know what they need but often policymakers fail to incorporate their lived experience," Chomilo said. "By prioritizing policy development through a racial equity lens and implementing it through a community co-created process, Minnesota Medicaid is building racial equity into the core of the healthcare system." On his LinkedIn page, Chomilo has called for ICE to be defunded, promoted a boycott of Target for ending DEI and lamented "Zionism in medicine today" in a recent Instagram post. Robbins told Fox News Digital that "clearly" Flanagan is "aligning herself with the most radical wing of the Democratic Party on health care and that is what she will bring to the US Senate." Nick Puglia, National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) regional press secretary, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Peggy Flanagan let fraudsters steal at least $9 billion from Minnesotans. Fundraising with those who perpetuated it is like handing lighter fluid to the arsonist who burned the house down." Fox News Digital reached out to the Flanagan campaign and Chomilo's office for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Polling shows that fraud is one of the top issues on the minds of voters heading into the November election, where Flanagan will face off against Republican Michele Tafoya. Tafoya has consistently hit Flanagan on fraud, citing the Democrat serving alongside Walz as his top lieutenant since 2019 as the fraud scandal unfolded. "I am appalled by the fraud that has occurred," Flanagan told Fox 9 Minneapolis in August. "Minnesotans are upset about it. They’re angry and I am too. I can tell you that this administration has taken steps. There’s a new office of inspector general that was passed this last legislative session. We’ve added staff to the attorney general’s office to root out Medicaid fraud. And, there was an aggressive action of shutting down a program that was being utilized by criminals. I think more absolutely needs to be done."

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: El-Sayed might have a problem with the Black vote in Michigan
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's support among Black voters in Michigan is dropping fast, and even a Kamala Harris campaign appearance may not fix the problem.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has a problem with a large slice of the state’s Black electorate. It doesn’t like him. That matters in a state where the voting population is 14% Black. (About 2% of Michigan voters are of Arab descent. 1.4% are Jewish.) BLACK VOTERS RIP DEMS OVER TAKING THEM FOR GRANTED IN EL-SAYED'S BACKYARD: ‘HUSH US UP’ In the most recent Washington Post–Schar School poll, Sept. 10–14, only 67% of likely Black Michigan voters supported El-Sayed. A Fox News poll from a month earlier, taken Aug. 6–10, found that 75% of Black Michigan voters said they would vote for El-Sayed. That is a trend in the wrong direction for El-Sayed. Two years ago, then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried the Black vote in Michigan with 87%. So, El-Sayed is significantly underperforming the most recent Democratic nominee for president. SOCIALIST POLITICIANS ARE 'MORE RACIST THAN THE KKK,' SAYS BLACK DEM OFFICIAL URGING VOTERS TO DITCH EL-SAYED The question is why is El-Sayed so weak with this particular demographic? El-Sayed has addressed this question very directly, including acknowledging that there is mistrust between parts of Detroit’s Black and Arab communities. El-Sayed may already have given up on Michigan’s significant Jewish vote coming around, but on Tuesday he campaigned with former Vice President Kamala Harris at an event aimed directly at Black women. It was an awkward "roundtable" that seemed to have been so narrowcasted at Black women as to have returned right out of peak Woke 1.0, which Congresswoman Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez assured us recently is an era behind us. Harris did not get that memo as her remarks Tuesday indicated. "The attack on DEI is an attack on maternal care," Harris opined as an uncomfortable-looking El-Sayed looked on, "including the need to protect Black women in connection with their pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care." The word salad chef of 2024 was back. HARRIS JOINS FORCES WITH RADICAL SENATE NOMINEE IN KEY SWING STATE AS 2028 WHISPERS SWIRL Whether or not the day’s appearance by the former VP helped El-Sayed at all with Black voters won’t be known for some time, but given the numbers in the public polling, El-Sayed had to try something to get Michigan’s crucial voting bloc at least start thinking about going to the polls in November even if that something was Harris, who has been notably absent from the critical Senate races until this week. There is little reason to believe that Harris is the answer to El-Sayed’s core problem. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES In an August 2026 interview with The Grio, El-Sayed was blunt about the Black-Arab-American divide in and around Detroit: "I think a lot of the mistrust among Black folk in Metro Detroit is well-founded, based on a kind of double standard that too often business owners, particularly in the Arab and, yes, Muslim communities have had when it comes to the way they do business in local communities," El-Sayed said. "You see money go in and then money leaves these communities rather than be reinvested in the community," El-Sayed continued. "It’s a conversation I’ve been having with the Arab and Muslim community for a very long time. We can’t sit here and talk about racism against Arabs and Muslims unless we’re willing to actually look inward and ask how is it that we’re engaging with the Black community in a way that is responsible?" So El-Sayed knows he has a problem with a key demographic. He has tried other approaches before bringing Harris into the state. El-Sayed declared he was open to "reparations" when he appeared with Fox News’ Jesse Watters, saying that an "incredible debt that was put upon Black folks as a function of slavery, that we have yet to pay." El-Sayed also told Watters the whole country should be discussing "how do we make people whole." The following month, El-Sayed was talking to leaders of the Black church, saying "unpaid debts" are owed to Black communities, debts that have "long since come due." BLACK CONSERVATIVE REVEALS HOW GOP CAN LOCK DOWN MINORITY VOTERS WITHOUT TRUMP ON BALLOT While the topic of "reparations" polls at 77% approval among Black Americans, only 18% of White voters support the concept. So the more El-Sayed pushes "reparations," the more likely he is to drive off the moderate independents already leery of his radical positions and friendship with Hasan Piker. Then there is the "Trump effect." President Trump collected 13% of the Black vote overall two years ago, and close to 20% of Black men. Does talk of DEI and maternal care at the El-Sayed-Harris roundtable Tuesday bring home votes among Black men? Does chatter about unspecified reparations even drive off the near quarter of the Black population that aren’t signed on to the concept? The long-standing tensions between the Black and Arab American communities in and around Detroit cannot be resolved in an election cycle that has focused on El-Sayed’s radical break with traditional Democratic campaign themes and profiles. El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, took more than two-thirds of Black voters in the primary. Republican nominee Mike Rogers knows this traditional Democratic stronghold is at least partially in play. We can’t see Team Rogers buy on "urban radio" or in other media serving the Black community, but we have seen Rogers making appearances throughout Wayne County and making many appearances with "Democrats for Rogers" groups featuring Black voters. Everyone knows that El-Sayed and his association with Hasan Piker has driven off the votes of a large number of Jewish Democrats. That the campaign is not connecting with Black voters as it must to give him a shot is the double nightmare for his campaign strategists. What can he do between now and November 3? It is hard to see a path to keep the moderate independent vote even as El-Sayed trots out traditional panders to the Black vote that don’t even resonate as credible or detailed. Even as El-Sayed struggles with basic messaging to core constituencies, Republican groups have poured more than $60 million into the Wolverine State. There are some polls showing El-Sayed with a lead over Rogers outside the margin of error. There were also lots of polls showing him winning the primary against Stevens by double digits, with one memorable miss putting him 18% up in a race he won by one point. The polling doesn’t add up given his problems with the Democratic base. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So stay focused on El-Sayed’s increasingly frenetic campaign and its sudden lurches here and there. There’s a reason radicals aren’t often nominated by major parties. Both Republican and Democratic Parties are built out of coalitions of interest groups. El-Sayed’s primary campaign fractured the traditional Democratic coalition. There is scant hard evidence that he has found a way to glue it back together again and then motivate it to vote between now and November 3.

articles.title: To the victor belong Venezuela’s spoils: Delcy Rodriguez’s UNGA about-face
articles.summary: Seven years after warning against US regime change, Venezuela’s interim president thanked the man who delivered it.
articles.body:
Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez took to the stage yesterday at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York City to deliver a rather bland speech, in which she thanked United States President Donald Trump for resuming “diplomatic relations and cooperation” with Venezuela.

This was a different vibe, to be sure, than the one she opted for at the same venue in September 2019, when, as vice president under Nicolas Maduro, she accused the US of perpetrating “economic terrorism” that did not require the use of bombs “but rather through banks and insurance companies”.

Denouncing the global superpower’s militarisation of international relations and punishment of millions of innocent people “in order to apply regime change doctrines and steal other nations’ resources”, the Rodriguez of 2019 went on to cite Venezuelan economic losses to the tune of $130bn between 2015 and 2018 alone on account of US sanctions.

She additionally offered her opinion that the domination of the US political system by “plutocratic minorities” made the country unqualified to impose its model on other countries.

Seven years later, US plutocracy is going strong with Trump at the helm – the same Trump alongside whom a grinning Rodriguez appeared in a photograph taken in New York on Tuesday, less than nine months after he oversaw regime change in Venezuela by kidnapping Maduro .

The kidnapped president is now also in New York, albeit in jail, and is scheduled to stand trial in June 2027 . This despite his attempts to remind everyone that, as a sitting head of state, his prosecution in a foreign court contravenes international law.

Then again, abducting other countries’ presidents is also pretty glaringly illegal. But Trump has made it clear that he alone is in charge of deciding what is and is not permissible on any given day.

The abduction took place on January 3, when the US military launched air attacks on Venezuela, killing some 100 people and whisking Maduro and his wife away.

He is accused of an array of misdeeds, including being the leader of the “Cartel of the Suns” – which, mind you, does not actually exist – and engaging in “conspiracy to possess machineguns and destructive devices”.

This is quite the accusation coming from the country that just used all manner of destructive devices to bomb Venezuela and kill a bunch of people.

Anyway, bald-faced hypocrisy is nothing new in the land of the “plutocratic minorities”.

Now, the waning corporate media interest in Maduro’s fate amounts to another coup for US impunity, as folks go about more or less forgetting that there is a foreign head of state sitting in a Brooklyn prison.

But Maduro’s disappearance works out well for Rodriguez, as she goes about enabling the very theft of resources she once decried.

Rodriguez took the stage at the UN the day after Trump, who used the platform to pat himself on the back for the trampling of Venezuelan sovereignty that conveniently culminated in last month’s announcement from the White House of the “biggest oil deal in world history”, securing US majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves.

Speaking to his international audience, Trump boasted: “To the victor belong the spoils. You’ve all heard that.”

Never mind that you’re not technically supposed to admit that you attacked a country just to get its oil. (You’re also not, in polite company, supposed to threaten to annihilate Iran – another of Trump’s UN talking points.)

Since January, the US has lifted many coercive economic measures against Venezuela (including against Rodriguez herself), easing the brutal sanctions regime that as of 2020 was estimated to have already killed 100,000 Venezuelans, according to former UN independent expert Alfred-Maurice de Zayas.

But trading sanctions for de facto colonialism isn’t a great deal, either.

Meanwhile, Trump’s continued manic bombing of vessels in the Caribbean and Pacific, which a recent UN report warned may constitute crimes against humanity, suggests the US is nowhere near to kicking its old habit of terrorism – and is all the more reason that Rodriguez might have refrained from thanking the US leader for his “cooperation”.

As Gregory Wilpert, founder of the Venezuelanalysis website and author of Changing Venezuela by Taking Power, diplomatically put it to me: “One cannot help but wonder whether Delcy Rodriguez is over-complying with Trump in some aspects of her negotiations with him.”

Noting that Rodriguez is “in a highly vulnerable position”, Wilpert ran through a few of the options she faces, such as “the possibility that the Trump administration could treat her as it treated Maduro – by attempting to kidnap her – or as it treated Iran, by targeting the country’s highest levels of government”.

Or, Wilpert said, there is always the Cuba approach, which would entail “the kind of economic siege” that is undertaken “with the aim of starving an entire country”.

In her UN address, Rodriguez promised that Venezuela would hold elections at some unspecified point in time – not that the US, for its part, really cares about democracy as long as the right people are in power.

And although it’s still too early to tell, Rodriguez might just be one of those people.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Trump disapproval highest in second term amid economic woes: Emerson College
articles.summary: President Trump’s disapproval rating hits the highest mark it has during his second White House stint amid rising energy costs and economic woes, according to a new poll. In an Emerson College poll, Trump’s disapproval rating hit 58 percent, while 39 percent of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of his job as president. The disapproval…
articles.body:
President Trump’s disapproval rating hits the highest mark it has during his second White House stint amid rising energy costs and economic woes , according to a new poll.

In an Emerson College poll, Trump’s disapproval rating hit 58 percent, while 39 percent of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of his job as president. The disapproval rating is 17 points higher than when Trump first took office in January 2025.

When asked how Trump has done in his second term so far, 56 percent responded he has done worse than expected, 26 percent said he has done better and 18 percent responded he has done as expected.

Compared to Emerson College’s 100 Day Poll from April 2025, those who say his performance is worse than expected increased from 43 percent, while those who say better decreased from 34 percent.

Sixty percent in the poll believe Trump’s economic policies are making the economy worse, while 28 percent think they are making it better and 13 percent think there is no effect or it is too soon to tell.

The president’s high disapproval rating comes as he faces criticism for the ongoing Iran war and widespread concern for his handling of the economy.

The national average price of gas is $4.47 per gallon as of Wednesday, according to AAA . Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane for oil exports, is the primary cause of higher prices in recent months.

The president brushed aside these rising costs, saying recently at a political rally in North Carolina that hiked gas prices were a “very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done.”

He is receiving backlash from figures within the GOP as Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wisc.), the Republican nominee in Wisconsin’s competitive gubernatorial race, called for the end to the military conflict against Iran.

Tiffany’s call was echoed by candidates in other battleground elections , such as Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

Trump told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that Iran faces a choice of either striking a deal with the U.S. to end the more than six-month war or face “ annihilation .”

The Emerson College Polling survey was conducted between Sept. 21-22 with 1,000 likely voters surveyed. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

articles.title: Beshear-Moore ticket? Democratic presidential hopefuls are pairing up
articles.summary: When Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) wanted to promote his new book this week, he invited Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) — one of his potential 2028 presidential rivals — to join him onstage and help moderate the event. On Tuesday night, the two governors appeared together before a Beltway crowd, with Moore giving Beshear…
articles.body:
When Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) wanted to promote his new book this week, he invited Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) — one of his potential 2028 presidential rivals — to join him onstage and help moderate the event.

On Tuesday night, the two governors appeared together before a Beltway crowd, with Moore giving Beshear a boost to plug his book and build his national audience.

“Our country needs you,” Moore told Beshear at one point, as the sold-out crowd gave him a standing ovation.

A year from now, when candidates are preparing for the first presidential primary contests, the tone and tenor between the two men may be a little different — at least if either or both are running for president. Beshear is widely seen as a prospective candidate, while Moore has repeatedly said he will not run for president in 2028.

The episode puts the spotlight on how Democrats eyeing a White House run are in an unusual period right now, where prospective rivals can still help one another garner attention and headlines ahead of the unofficial start of the primary race. That will be sometime after the midterm elections.

In some cases, it could also be an initial testing of the waters for potential running mates, as was the case at Tuesday’s event.

“Based on the time we’ve been here tonight, I think we make a pretty good team,” Beshear told Moore.

“At this point, everyone is looking for attention,” Democratic strategist Jamal Simmons said. “Doing events together is helpful to everyone. It doesn’t cost you anything and you might pick up some attention you otherwise wouldn’t get.”

The double auditions are happening elsewhere, too. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) last month interviewed Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) on his podcast, where he needled her about running for president as the two drank beer at a Michigan bar.

During their conversation, Newsom sought to egg on Whitmer, nudging her to confess that she’s thinking about running for president. Whitmer shook her head and smiled as her California counterpart came back with, “The pause says it all.”

Last month, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) appeared on a three-day swing in Georgia with Democratic colleague Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.), who is campaigning for reelection. The joint appearances had political observers wondering if they were seeing what could be a preview of a 2028 Democratic ticket.

When a Politico reporter asked Kelly if their appearances foreshadowed an “Ossoff-Kelly” ticket, the Arizona senator replied, “Hey, why’d you put it in that order?”

“We’re seeing the linking up and teaming up and buddying up right now because as soon as Election Day happens, I don’t think we get to Thanksgiving before hearing announcements,” said one Democratic strategist who plans to be involved in the presidential race.

“I do think that Democrats are in a movement-building moment, and when you’re in that moment, you’re going to find spaces to be allies and lean into existing relationships to test the waters,” they said. “This is a new era in the party, and new relationships and alliances are being formed.”

The strategist compared it to athletes who play on different teams.

“It doesn’t mean they won’t go hard on each other when the game begins,” they said. “But right now, they probably don’t mind breaking the fourth wall every now and again and seeing what attention comes from it.”

During Tuesday’s event in Washington, Beshear reiterated a story he’s told in recent months in speeches and interviews about how he thought his 2023 gubernatorial reelection campaign would be his final race.

“Sitting here today, I’m not sure that’s true,” Beshear told Moore, who is up for reelection himself in November. “And while that is not any sort of announcement, because that would require me to fill out paperwork, I just won’t leave a broken country to my kids or to our future generations.”

A RealClearPolitics average of national polling shows a wide-open race for the field of would-be Democratic presidential candidates.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who sources say is considering whether to mount another race, leads the average polls by 10 points with 24 percent, while Newsom comes in second with nearly 14 percent.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is third with 13.1 percent, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) is at 11 percent and Ossoff follows with 9 percent.

Beshear, who is in the top 10 of the RealClearPolitics average, hinted Tuesday that he’ll have some competition — possibly from Moore, and others — if he does decide to make it official and jump in the race.

“We may have a lot of great candidates,” he said.

articles.title: GOP breaks ranks on Iran as voters fume over war’s costs
articles.summary: Republican support for the war in Iran is dropping as Senate GOP candidates speak out against it and voters increasingly blame high gas prices on the nearly seven-month conflict. Growing public opposition among even Republican voters has put incumbents such as Sens. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Pete Ricketts…
articles.body:
Republican support for the war in Iran is dropping as Senate GOP candidates speak out against it and voters increasingly blame high gas prices on the nearly seven-month conflict.

Growing public opposition among even Republican voters has put incumbents such as Sens. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) in a tough political position.

Several of these Republican candidates, including Husted; former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), who is running for Senate in Michigan; and Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate in Iowa, are calling for a swift end to the war.

“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Rogers urged in a campaign video Monday.

Hinson on Monday wrote on social media that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”

Husted told Politico on Tuesday that “the war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices.”

The calls are also coming from the lower chamber.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) in an interview with a local TV station urged “a resolution” to the war.

Recent polls show that Rogers and Husted are trailing their Democratic opponents, Abdul El-Sayed and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio), respectively.

Hinson, meanwhile, is locked in a tough race the Cook Political Report last month shifted to “toss-up.”

A Republican senator who requested anonymity to discuss voter frustration over the war and high gas prices said there’s growing political pressure on GOP candidates to oppose the unpopular conflict.

“People are very, very concerned about costs. They associate higher fuel costs with the Iran war, directly. Farmers are very, very concerned. All their input costs are being driven up. It’s a problem,” the senator said.

Hinson on Monday wrote that “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said Wednesday there are “a lot of Republicans” who want to end the war as quickly as possible.

“Everybody wants to see wars come to a conclusion,” he said. “We are hopeful that the administration’s efforts will lead to getting the Strait of Hormuz open, getting the shipping lanes open and taking some of the pressure off of the American people’s pocketbooks.”

“We want to see that conflict come to an end,” he said. “I think the administration is working aggressively to make that happen.”

Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) called the conflict “a quagmire” but warned that President Trump can’t simply walk away while Iran still has a path to obtain nuclear weapons.

“All of us want it to end as soon as possible,” he said. “Our president decided we needed to go [to war] and we went, and I was fully supportive of going.

“Unexpected things come up within war,” he added. “Now we’re in a quagmire to some degree and energy prices are high. … This thing has turned into something [Trump] didn’t expect — none of us expected this, that this would go on this long.”

Democrats are expected to force a vote later this week on a House-passed concurrent resolution ordering Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict.

The measure is expected to pick up more Republican support, and a source familiar with the whip count said it has a good chance of passing.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) now says he will vote for the war powers resolution directing Trump to end the conflict.

“We’re reaching a point to where we just need answers. We got to know what success looks like,” Tillis said.

Tillis wants the Trump administration to lay out its plan for concluding the war and to ask for a formal authorization to continue the conflict.

“There’s never been any way to measure what success looks like,” he said. “For every step we take forward, we take a step back.”

He warned that the war has become a major political problem for Senate GOP candidates and the broader Republican Party.

Tillis said Republicans have seen “consistently downward-trending negative reaction since” the first strikes against Iran in February.

“We don’t know how long it’s going to go,” he said. “So we’re afraid it could be a forever war. It’s a war that’s obviously hurting people economically. Why are we doing this? What is the goal?”

Tillis said support for the war among Republican voters is dropping significantly.

A CNN poll conducted by SSRS of 1,206 U.S. adults nationwide found that support for the war among self-identified Republicans has dropped by more than 10 percentage points since March.

Six months ago, 73 percent of surveyed Republicans approved of Trump’s handling of the conflict, but that number has since dropped to 60 percent.

A Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters nationwide conducted Sept. 11-14 found that 71 percent of voters think Trump doesn’t have a clear strategy for ending the war.

Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Rand Paul (R-Ky.) are expected to vote later this week for the Democrat-sponsored war powers resolution. They have voted several times previously for Iran-related war powers measures.

A Republican senator who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations said other GOP colleagues could “flip” on the Iran war powers resolution.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) is hinting he may also vote for it, complaining that there has been “very little” to “no” consultation with Congress about ending the conflict.

Centrist Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), who has repeatedly voted against war powers resolutions related to Iran, is expected to vote this week with Republicans against the measure.

Republican senators on Wednesday urged their colleagues in tough races — or candidates in battleground states such as Michigan — to say what they need to about the war to win in November.

“If I’m running in an environment like this, obviously you’re going to develop a campaign and a message that can win in your state. I encourage most candidates to run their own campaigns,” Thune said when asked about the calls from Rogers and Hinson to bring the Iran conflict to a swift end.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said GOP candidates “are responding to their voters.”

“They got to listen to their constituents and be responsive,” he said.

articles.title: On Capitol Hill, the reporters run free. GOP senators are fine with it
articles.summary: President Trump has barred news outlets from the White House, and a prominent GOP congresswoman is making noise about restricting press access to parts of the Capitol. But Republicans in the Senate, where reporters have more direct access to lawmakers than anywhere in Washington, say they’re content with the status quo. Senate Majority Leader John…
articles.body:
President Trump has barred news outlets from the White House, and a prominent GOP congresswoman is making noise about restricting press access to parts of the Capitol.

But Republicans in the Senate, where reporters have more direct access to lawmakers than anywhere in Washington, say they’re content with the status quo.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said the “courts will decide” the rightness of Trump’s move, but banning certain outlets is “not my policy.”

In fact, Congress allows reporters broad and generally indiscriminate access to speak directly with members of both chambers every day.

The general public can freely access the hallways of the office buildings in the House and Senate, and reporters — who are credentialed by the nonpartisan press galleries — are allowed almost everywhere that staff are throughout the Capitol, including most underground trains, tunnels and staircases that members use to get around.

And while there have historically been efforts to restrict or change access to the Capitol, Republican lawmakers who spoke to The Hill generally maintained that they’re comfortable with the freedom of movement reporters have.

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said he’s been “thinking a lot about” Trump’s move, because he’s had problems with certain outlets being “incredibly untruthful in their reporting,” causing him to decline to comment for their stories.

“So I understand the emotion of it,” Lankford said. “The challenge is they’ve got to have some kind of access because they still have [to be able] to report a story, especially if you’re a pool. We got to be able to have that.”

When The Hill asked if he was comfortable with how much access reporters have to senators, he said he was. He said banning outlets from the building entirely, as Trump did, is different than letting reporters into the Capitol, where lawmakers can still decline to answer questions if upset with the coverage.

“They have access to the building, but I’m just not going to answer the question because I just can’t trust what’s going to run,” Lankford said.

Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.), chair of the House Rules Committee, made headlines last week when she said many lawmakers are “irritated” with the presence of reporters in the Speaker’s Lobby, a narrow room directly off the House floor where members wander, take meetings and calls, and sometimes rest on benches in between votes. That space has been closed to the press for periods in the past, including the COVID-19 pandemic, but was reopened in 2021.

Besides Foxx, even Republicans who support Trump’s right to ban certain outlets aren’t looking to do the same around the Capitol. Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) told The Hill that “that’s his option,” and that “he’s probably tired of the fake news.”

“I’m fine with it, but he deals with 100 times more than we do,” Tuberville said of press access in the Senate.

The three outlets that Trump blocked — Politico, MS NOW and CNN — presented arguments in court against the move on Wednesday. A judge initially seemed skeptical of the administration’s case.

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) told reporters he expected the White House press ban problem to get resolved quickly and that it is just Trump sending a message about coverage.

“I think he’s sending them a message like, ‘Hey, be fair.’ And I think at some point they’ll be able to cover him, and we’ll move on. That’s my guess.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) a retiring Republican who is regularly swamped with crowds of reporters as he’s become more prone to criticizing the Trump administration, told reporters Tuesday that Trump’s move to limit the press corps over unfavorable reporting is “silly.”

“The American people don’t like that,” Tillis said.

“Didn’t work for Victor Orbán … it hasn’t worked for [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth. Look, be proud of what you have to say. Have a counter. I mean, every discussion with the press should be like a good debate. If you’ve been doing your job, you should be able to pivot and either discredit the question or have compelling information for why the premise of the question is wrong. But to just eliminate people because they don’t give you favorable reviews or favorable questions to me is silly.”

articles.title: Democrats hold 11-point lead over GOP on congressional ballot: Poll
articles.summary: Democrats hold a comfortable 11-point lead over Republicans on a generic congressional ballot, according to new poll — the latest survey showing enduring Democratic momentum ahead of November. An Emerson College Polling survey released on Thursday found Democrats led Republicans 53 percent to 42 percent on a generic congressional ballot test. A similar survey…
articles.body:
Democrats hold a comfortable 11-point lead over Republicans on a generic congressional ballot, according to new poll — the latest survey showing enduring Democratic momentum ahead of November.

An Emerson College Polling survey released on Thursday found Democrats led Republicans 53 percent to 42 percent on a generic congressional ballot test. A similar survey released last month showed Democrats with an 8-point lead — 51 percent to Republicans’ 43 percent.

“While the generic ballot test doesn’t capture nuances of individual races, it’s an important metric to gauge the magnitude of a potential Democratic wave,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, explained in a Thursday press release.

“Independent and Hispanic voters, who broke for President Trump in 2024, support the Democratic candidate by significant margins, 60 percent to 31 percent and 64 percent to 31 percent, respectively.”

The national poll showed Trump with a 39 percent approval rating compared to a nearly 58 percent disapproval rating. Fifty-six percent of respondents said that Trump had done worse than expected in his second term, while 26 percent said he did better than expected and close to 18 percent said it was about what they expected.

When respondents were asked about how important certain issues were to them at the ballot box, the Iran war, jobs and tariff policy ranked as the top three issues.

Thursday’s survey offers the latest warning sign for Republicans less than two months from the midterm elections. Trump’s approval ratings have continued to decline, while the high cost of living — impacted by the war in Iran as well as the Trump administration’s tariff policies — are even rankling Republicans.

Several GOP House and Senate candidates have spoken out against the conflict in the Middle East in recent days. Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) put out an ad this week calling for the end of the war with Iran amid concerns over higher diesel and grocery prices, while Iowa’s GOP Senate pick, Rep. Ashley Hinson, has echoed these concerns.

The Emerson College Polling survey was conducted between Sept. 21-22 with 1,000 likely voters surveyed. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

"Now, you don't need me to tell you that communism is making a comeback right now in our country," Barron said in front of the Gateway Arch on Tuesday. "And I think especially churchmen need, like Sheen, to raise their voices against it and, furthermore, as American churchmen, to speak out strongly on both American and Catholic principles against the re-emergence of this still very dangerous ideology." BISHOP BARRON SLAMS 'BORDERLINE COMMUNISTS' SANDERS, MAMDANI AHEAD OF TRUMP PRAYER EVENT: 'ECONOMY THAT KILLS' Sheen, an author and television personality who became one of the Catholic Church's most prominent voices in the 20th century, will be beatified at The Dome at America's Center. The Vatican approved Sheen's beatification in 2019 after recognizing a miracle involving the unexplained recovery of James Fulton Engstrom, a baby born without a pulse in 2010, according to The Associated Press. In addition to serving as a Catholic bishop, Barron said Sheen was also "a very proud American." BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: MY YEAR WITH DOJ'S RELIGIOUS LIBERTY COMMISSION: WHY I SAID YES Turning to the Declaration of Independence, Barron said Sheen argued communism, rooted in Karl Marx's teachings, also threatened the foundations of equality, freedom and individual rights.
