articles.title: Daughter of Chinese Uyghur prisoner makes emotional plea to Trump during spotlight Xi summit
articles.summary: Ziba Murat hopes Trump will raise her mother Dr. Gulshar Abbas' case with Xi Jinping during the summit after eight years of imprisonment in China.
articles.body: An American woman whose mother has been wrongfully imprisoned in China for eight years is hoping that President Donald Trump will ask Chinese leader Xi Jinping for clemency during the high-profile ongoing summit between the pair of world leaders Thursday. "We are doing everything we can to bring this in front of President Trump, and I know that if he knows about this case, he will care about this case," Ziba Murat told Fox News Digital in an emotional interview on her mother's continued imprisonment. "I hope we are pulling the right levers and President Trump can bring her home." Dr. Gulshar Abbas is Murat's mother. She was 56 when she disappeared from her home on Sept. 10, 2018. In December of that year, according to Murat, Chinese government officials confirmed in a press conference that Abbas was convicted on charges of taking part in organized terrorism, aiding terrorist activities and seriously disrupting social order — charges Murat describes as "made up" — and was sentenced to 20 years in prison. CHINA’S XI SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE "Her disappearance came six days after her sister, my aunt Rushan Abbas, spoke ... about what's happening to the Uyghur people back home, and then the Chinese government picked her up six days after," said Murat. "We didn't see it coming, honestly, because she is a retired doctor. She's not a political person. She's not an activist. She's just a grandma and, you know — it took us almost two years to find out what happened to her [and] where she's being held." Rushan Abbas runs Campaign for Uyghurs, a large nonprofit advocacy group for the Muslim minority population in China, which has been subject to brutal oppression at the hands of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). MOTHER RECOUNTS HORRORS OF BRUTAL CHINESE DETENTION CAMP WHERE INFANT SON DIED Abbas' case is a prominent one. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has used his position and official office to advocate on her behalf. Murat was the Republican leader's guest at the 2026 State of the Union speech. But progress in freeing her mother has been an uphill battle, considering the secretive nature of the Chinese government and tensions with the United States over issues like trade and intellectual property theft, among many others. Murat is hoping that some of that tension will abate after Thursday's bilateral summit, and that by the end of the day, she'll be one step closer to seeing her mother again. TRUMP-XI SUMMIT SHOULD MAKE SURE AMERICAN STRENGTH DELIVERS AMERICAN RESULTS Through tears, Murat described life without her mother, noting that she's missing out on precious memories with her family, 24 of whom are United States citizens. Murat's daughter was only 3 months old when Abbas disappeared. "It's been hard because, like I said, I was a new mom myself when all this started happening," she said. "And my sister had her second baby four weeks after ... my mom's disappearance." Her daughter, now 8, is starting to ask questions about her grandmother. "Just a couple of months ago, we were reading a book ... [the] encyclopedia for kids, and they have the pages of [the] family tree," Abbas said. "So we're going over, you know, talking about my husband's parents and then my parents, and she just sat there and looked at me. She's like, 'I saw aunt Rushan has grandma Gulshar's picture ... [and] it says my sister is gone.' Where is grandma?" Murat is trying hard to withhold the real answer to that question, and tells her daughter that Abbas is far away, and the family is hoping that she can come meet her soon. But with all the meetings Murat attends and the people with whom she discusses the case, her young daughter is starting to catch on. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "She just lets out this big sigh, and she's like, 'Oh, okay.' I thought she was in jail,'" Murat explained. "Even without me telling her, she started to pick up things, and it just breaks my heart to see her, and I don't have answer to provide her on when her grandma will be home. So it's very frustrating." A senior White House official confirmed to Fox News on Wednesday that Trump is expected to ask Xi to release at least one prisoner, U.S. citizen Dr. Youlin Chen, who was arrested outside a Beijing airport by Chinese officials in 2024. articles.title: Trump-Xi reunion comes with unfinished business — and a bigger battle looming
articles.summary: President Donald Trump hosts Xi Jinping to test whether China delivered on rare earths, AI and trade promises from their May breakthrough deal.
articles.body: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for a summit with President Donald Trump, four months after the two leaders reached a sweeping agreement that included Chinese commitments on rare earths, agricultural purchases, trade and investment. Trump hailed that agreement as a breakthrough for American farmers, manufacturers and workers. But the latest talks come amid uneven progress on commitments involving rare-earth minerals, agricultural and commercial purchases, trade and investment, while key disputes over tariffs, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, intellectual property and Taiwan remain unresolved. Under the May agreement, China committed to address U.S. concerns over rare-earth supplies and purchase at least $17 billion a year in U.S. agricultural products, while also approving an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft, restoring market access for American beef and resuming poultry imports. The two countries also chartered new boards on trade and investment. CHINA’S XI SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE Four months later, implementation has been uneven. Reuters reported that China is making progress toward finalizing its commitment to purchase 200 Boeing jets, while agricultural imports are projected to fall short of the agreed level and the new trade and investment boards are still being put into operation. AI is expected to be a major focus of the two-day summit, along with possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods and discussions over China’s rare-earth exports, according to a senior administration official. The May agreement, when Trump and Xi last met, also chartered new U.S.-China boards on trade and investment, though it did not resolve the broader economic and national security tensions between the two countries. REalloys CEO Lipi Sternheim told Fox News Digital China’s dominance of the rare-earth supply chain gives Beijing leverage over U.S. defense and technology industries, warning that the Trump-Xi meeting must preserve supplies while American production ramps up. "The fact that Trump and Xi are meeting and the main topic of the day is rare earths probably tells you and the American people all they need to know about the importance," said Sternheim. Sternheim said the immediate goal of the Trump-Xi meeting should be to keep rare earths flowing to U.S. defense manufacturers for the next two to three years, giving American companies time to build domestic mining, processing and magnet-making capacity and reduce their dependence on China. THE WEST STILL DOESN’T GRASP THE DANGER OF CHINA’S RARE EARTH ENDGAME He said that rare earth minerals are used to make the powerful magnets found in cellphones, electric vehicles, drones, robots and defense systems, including missiles, F-35 fighter jets, submarines and missile-defense systems. Heavy rare earths are especially important for high-temperature applications such as missiles and space systems, but China controls most of the mining, processing and magnet-making capacity. Sternheim cautioned that shifting production to the U.S. will not happen quickly. "You can’t build 40 years in two days," Sternheim said, adding that it will take years. Trump touted the U.S. lead over China in artificial intelligence during an address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, while declaring that U.S. government documents would begin referring to the technology as "superintelligence." AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD "Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," said Trump. "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. That's the group that wins. And we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else. And we're going to keep it that way." While Trump and Xi will be in meetings, first lady Melania Trump is expected to accompany Xi’s wife Peng to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art. The two will "explore works spanning centuries of artistic achievement and Sino-American cultural exchange." Thursday will begin with a prestigious State Arrival Ceremony, including 479 military personnel from all branches on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House. The day will end with a state dinner with high-profile guests, including many from the tech world. Those guests will include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former senior White House adviser Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP House Speaker Mike Johnson will also be in attendance, a source familiar told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Are the Russians coming?
articles.summary: Winter is soon coming, and so too is a growing dread across Europe. It is dawning on European capitals that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s only conventional path to victory in Ukraine may lie through the Baltic States. Kyiv’s fortress Donbas in eastern Ukraine remains largely impenetrable. Despite Russian claims in advance of last week’s Duma elections that…
articles.body:
Winter is soon coming, and so too is a growing dread across Europe. It is dawning on European capitals that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s only conventional path to victory in Ukraine may lie through the Baltic States.

Kyiv’s fortress Donbas in eastern Ukraine remains largely impenetrable. Despite Russian claims in advance of last week’s Duma elections that it had seized 5,300 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory, the reality is far more humiliating. According to the Institute for the Study of War, Putin’s army has only managed to capture only 147.7 square kilometers , and at an appalingly high cost — 314,530 Russian casualties this year to date, according to the latest Ukrainian estimates .

That backs Putin into a corner, which should alarm everyone.

Moscow needs another way to get to Kyiv — especially since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky – no matter how many times President Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff or Jared Kushner foolishly ask — is not going to give it to Putin without a fight. He would be committing national suicide, giving up a region that is essential to Ukraine’s defense.

But if not through the Donbas, then how can Putin win? So far, to hedge his bets in Ukraine, he has directed the Kremlin to wage an asymmetrical war against the European Union and NATO member states. Increasingly, that war has become kinetic as evinced by the armed drone placed next to a Ukrainian cargo jet at the Halle Airport in Leipzig, Germany.

Berlin accused Russia of responsibility. Putin, in turn, claimed Germany had fabricated the incident to blame Moscow.

Putin’s decision to respond directly was noteworthy. Reading between the lines, he wanted Berlin to see what Moscow is doing. In effect, despite his denial, Putin is signaling that he intends to increase Russian hybrid attacks against Europe.

Europe is finally sounding the alarm. Last Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron called a hastily arranged emergency meeting of France’s top political leaders. He urgently warned that “no one is safe” given Putin’s goal of finding new ways “to intimidate us and break our support for the Ukrainians.”

Europe has not been safe. As we have long argued, Putin has been at war with the West ever since he invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Ever since, on an increasing basis, Moscow has been conducting a grey-zone war in the open against Europe via sabotage , espionage , assassination , and election interference .

Thus far, Putin’s hybrid war in Europe has only produced small returns. Although it has failed to get Brussels or the major powers — including France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom — to back down, it has created growing political divisions within the NATO alliance and the European Union.

Using Russian gas and oil, Moscow succeeded in intimidating Slovakia and Hungary into effective geopolitical submission. Both countries repeatedly obstruct military and economic aid for Ukraine. To date, they have thwarted Ukraine’s accession talks to join NATO as well as the European Union.

Yet at best, those Russian successes have been speedbumps. Putin needs a bigger return from both countries if he is to succeed in cutting off European support for Ukraine. One way for the Kremlin to achieve this would be to attack the Baltics, militarily dividing NATO in the process.

Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico recklessly played into this scenario when he told medical students, “I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article five.” Article five is the collective NATO defense clause originally designed to protect Europe from a Russian invasion. In denying his intention to respond appropriately to a Russian attack on his NATO allies, Fico planted a large Russian target on Lithuania, Estonia, or Latvia’s back, and potentially Poland’s as well.

Moscow does not have to conduct a full-scale ground invasion of the Baltic States to try to change the equation. Simply launching a large drone and ballistic missile attack, precipitated by a Russian false-flag event, would suffice.

Putin would be counting on NATO being paralyzed and failing to respond. If so, Brussels would rethink its support for Ukraine.

Europe is clearly worried about this very scenario becoming a reality. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned about it. So too did Michal Koudelka , the head of the Czech Republic’s security service.

Are the Russians coming to Western Europe? Maybe — and maybe sooner than Finnish President Alexander Stubb believes. He warned against overreacting to Russia’s growing kinetic attacks against Europe. In our view, he is getting it wrong.

Europe, to deter Putin in the Baltic States, must go on the offensive. Implementing an active defense would be one way for Europe to signal to Putin that it has no intention of backing down in its support of Ukraine.

NATO — or a coalition of the willing — could declare an active defense zone over Western Ukraine and make it clear they will shoot down any Russian drone or ballistic missile before they can approach European territory.

Putin is expanding his kinetic war to Europe. To counter it and forestall any Russian attack on the Baltic States, Europe must expand its defense of Ukraine.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: The enemy within the judicial gates
articles.summary: Judges’ views on climate change are being influenced by an organization bragging that its purpose is to build and enable “a network of judges and scientists advancing climate science education for the judiciary.”
articles.body:
Chief Justice John Roberts famously identified violence, intimidation, disinformation, and defying lawfully entered judgements as four areas encroaching on the independence of judges. Now there’s a fifth: calculated infiltration of the judicial system to influence case outcomes.

After tobacco litigation culminated in multibillion dollar settlements, trial lawyers lit upon climate change as a potentially lucrative new area for liability claims. With the U.S. oil and gas industry generating average annual revenues of around $1.3 trillion, the profitability of such lawsuits was obvious.

More than 3,300 climate change cases later, activist allies assessed that the best way to get judges to agree on a deep-pocketed culprit for something as amorphous and evolving as the weather is to “educate” the judges.

Judges’ views on climate change are being influenced by seminars given by the Environmental Law Institute’s Climate Judiciary Project, which brags that their purpose is to build and enable “a network of judges and scientists advancing climate science education for the judiciary.” It is taken by judges who may oversee cases in which plaintiffs allege injuries from the manufacturing, marketing, use or sale of fossil-fuel products. Such “education” leaves them vulnerable to charges of bias.

More than 2,000 judges have participated since 2018, though their names and testimonials were anonymized or removed once attention was brought to possible conflict of interest. At least two judges who presided over climate cases have been publicly identified as being involved with Environmental Law Institute education and events. Furthermore, this education was financially supported by multiple groups who also give millions to the very law firm bringing the litigation before the courts, Sher Edling.

Another attempt to influence judicial views popped up in the latest edition of the Federal Judicial Center’s Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence. This volume included, for the first time, a chapter on climate science.

“It amounts to a sweeping brief intended to influence judges to think every harm from climate change is the result of fossil fuels,” said the Wall Street Journal . The volume’s climate chapter “was an abuse of science by political actors who tried to hijack a tool of judicial education to serve the interests of the plaintiffs’ bar in the cause of bankrupting fossil-fuel energy companies.”

Disturbingly, textual analysis indicates that one of those actors appears to be Michael Burger, who is both executive director of Columbia’s Sabin Center for Climate Change law and of counsel at Sher Edling.

Though the Federal Judicial Center removed the chapter from their online version, publication partner National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has retained it, leaving open the question of which version of the manual is authoritative. It is unclear which version will be or was shipped to judges, even after Trump recently called on federal suspension and debarment officials to review conduct of officials at the academies.

External groups seeking to take over judges’ views is one form of infiltration. Another, more sinister form, is demonstrated in the undermining of objectivity on the bench. Judges overseeing cases involving Trump have allowed their personal feelings to go unchecked. The unfortunate result is that rulings betray their adversarial posture toward Trump, which undermines the appearance of impartiality. As an example, U.S. District Judge William Young quoted Shakespeare and his own wife in calling Trump a tyrant. Incendiary statements like these makes it look like a judge is on a personal mission, supposedly to save the world from Trump.

Some federal district court judges have gone so far as to openly defy the orders of the United States Supreme Court. This led Justice Neil Gorsuch to write of these instances, “Lower court judges may sometimes disagree with this court’s decisions, but they are never free to defy them.”

When judges inject their personal views into a case, or law firms entice state officials to misuse their positions, our judicial system suffers. Courts, as an institution, rely on public trust. To preserve that trust, judges must make every effort to show the public that they are fair—that they have not made up their minds before they hear the case based on who the parties are or what they personally think is the right decision. When that fundamental perception of fairness is lost, public trust is broken.

As Roberts advised , when our judicial system is distorted “in ways that compromise the public’s confidence in our processes and outcomes, we must as a nation publicize the risks and take all appropriate measures to stop them.”

Judges who obviously inject personal views and political perspectives into their decisions must be forced to publicly answer for their improper conduct. Currently, any member of the public can file a complaint with a state judicial conduct commission or the relevant appellate court. At the federal level, these complaints are adjudicated only by other judges. This should change to include lay members of the public, similar to Arizona’s commission on judicial conduct.

Let public accountability begin to reinforce private trust.

Andrew Gould is a partner at Holtzman Vogel and a former Arizona Supreme Court justice.

articles.title: Five questions hanging over Trump’s meeting with Xi
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Xi’s state visit kicks off ▪ Judge strikes down media ban ▪ Debate over how to tackle diesel costs ▪ Forecasters shift races toward Democrats Chinese President Xi Jinping is meeting with President Trump today for high-stakes talks that could touch on several points of tension between their countries, including artificial intelligence…
articles.body:
▪ Debate over how to tackle diesel costs

▪ Forecasters shift races toward Democrats

Chinese President Xi Jinping is meeting with President Trump today for high-stakes talks that could touch on several points of tension between their countries, including artificial intelligence and weapons shipments to Taiwan.

The state visit is Xi’s first to the U.S. in a decade, coming just four months after Trump’s own visit to China in May. The pair of global leaders appeared to improve relations during that summit, though there were few signs of progress on a trade deal.

The world will be watching closely to see if the pomp and pageantry leads to any breakthroughs this time around.

Here’s five questions surrounding Trump’s meeting with Xi:

The rising fears around the growth of AI have added to the anticipation around the superpower summit, with members of both parties expressing concern about the technology getting out of control.

Trump’s approach to the concerns has largely been to brush them aside, emphasizing that the U.S. must win an AI arms race with China, which is viewed as the U.S.’s top competitor. One safeguard that the administration seems to be open to is the creation of an AI hotline to establish a point of cooperation between the U.S. and China.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters Sunday that the U.S. had proposed a “notification mechanism” for the countries to share when an AI incident happens that could affect national security. The proposal is reminiscent of the “red phone” that the U.S. and Soviet Union used to communicate in emergency situations during the Cold War.

“We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats,” Bessent said after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. “We think that just like any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important.”

Given Trump’s resistance to AI regulation and interest in one-upping China, the hotline may be the best hope for concrete cooperation, at least for now.

Will there be progress on a broader trade deal?

Just ahead of the meeting between Trump and Xi, Bessent announced Wednesday that officials agreed on an extension of their trade truce into January.

Trump and Xi reached an agreement last October to ease tensions of the trade war between their nations, but they were unable to make progress on a broader deal during the May summit in Beijing.

The truce was set to expire on Nov. 10. Under the truce, the Trump administration agreed to reduce tariffs on Chinese goods, while China agreed to delay export controls on rare earths and resume some soybean purchases.

An agreement to extend the current terms staves off the resumption of a full-scale trade war like what the U.S. is currently facing with Canada. But the true prize would be a comprehensive trade agreement to settle tensions for the long term, which has proven elusive so far.

Bessent raised some doubts about the potential of achieving a wider deal during a Fox News interview Wednesday.

“I don’t know whether a bigger deal can be done. I don’t know whether we will just roll the current deal,” he said , noting the extension could give leaders more time to negotiate.

Will Trump call out China’s support for Iran?

The president has been eager for any development that can shake up the stalemate that’s been in place in the Iran conflict for months, and his meeting with Xi may be a prime opportunity to try.

Trump has repeatedly urged countries around the world to sever economic ties with Tehran.

Bessent issued a global warning in August telling countries with any financial ties to Iran to cut off the regime or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system. He didn’t call out any specific countries at the time, but China remains Iran’s largest trading partner and primary destination for its oil exports.

The administration had earlier sanctioned Chinese entities processing Iranian oil. China denounced Bessent’s announcement as only further inflaming tensions, a sign of how any push from Trump may play with Beijing.

The president also has a new weapon to use against China, after signing into law a tariffs and sanctions bill named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) earlier this month. The bill gives him authorities to punish countries doing the most trade with Russia, including China.

The status of Taiwan is a perennial issue any time that U.S. and Chinese leaders meet, and eyes will be on whether Trump signals any shift in U.S. posture on arming the island against a potential Chinese invasion.

Beijing has long pushed for the U.S. to recognize Taiwan as part of China, considering it to be awaiting reunification with mainland China. The U.S. is pledged under federal law to provide Taiwan with support in the event of any invasion but keeps its plans ambiguous on whether it would defend the island itself.

Possible new arms funding to Taiwan hangs in the balance, with Trump weighing whether to greenlight a $14 billion arms package.

A senior administration official told NewsNation’s Hannah Brandt that Trump will decide “in fairly short time.” The package is expected to be a topic that comes up during his meeting with Xi, with the Chinese leader having previously asked him to pause the sale.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and three other Republican senators called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to release the stalled financial assistance in a letter Wednesday, reminding them of their past statements supporting Taiwan’s sovereignty.

Still, Rubio said the U.S. is partially constrained in its abilities by Washington’s potential needs in other parts of the world, arguing the pause isn’t specifically about Taiwan.

Will China commit to releasing political prisoners?

Trump has found success on multiple occasions in making deals to get Americans and others the U.S. considers wrongfully detained freed, and the families of those held in Chinese custody are hoping he can reach a deal again.

The Hill’s Laura Kelly and Julia Manchester reported last month on several notable Americans being held in China whose families are looking to Trump’s “unique” diplomacy as a way to get their relatives home.

One of the most high-profile prisoners is Jimmy Lai , a Hong Kong pro-democracy leader who is serving a long prison sentence for violations of the region’s national security law.

But Xi has often shown resistance to letting these types of prisoners go.

Mike Lillis , one of The Hill’s House reporters, has his own look at five critical issues that lawmakers want Trump to raise with Xi, getting more in depth to these questions and others. Subscribe to The Hill Insider to read Mike’s analysis here .

Forty days remain until voters hit the polls across America to decide the balance of power. I spoke with Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters and asked him how many seats he believes Republicans end up winning. He had specific numbers in mind.

“I say we pick up let’s say, 220 seats in the House. I hate to give predictions, so these are what I think. I think we end up at 53 Senate seats. We stay even,” Gruters added. “We have a lot more resources to spend. We’ve been holding out, and then we have our secret weapon in President Donald J. Trump,” he added.

What stood out to me was that Gruters was predicting a tight finish. That stands in contrast to the feeling right now among Democrats, many of whom believe they are on the verge of a potential blue wave, especially given the backdrop of war and high gas prices .

BATTED DOWN: A federal judge ordered the White House to immediately restore press credentials to CNN, MS NOW and Politico early Thursday, finding the administration’s ban likely violated their constitutional due process rights.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly , a Trump appointee, expressed heavy skepticism about the legality of the ban during a hearing Wednesday afternoon, saying early on that due process “wasn’t followed here.” He didn’t initially rule from the bench but said he would issue a decision soon.

“Defendants do not dispute that Plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked,” Kelly wrote.

The three outlets sued after Trump announced they would be barred from White House grounds. The administration later sent the outlets letters pointing to national security concerns.

Kelly found he’s bound by a 1977 precedent that the Fifth Amendment’s due process protections come into play when the White House arbitrarily denies a credential to reporters.

Theodore Boutrous , an attorney for the media outlets, argued the ban amounted to “viewpoint discrimination” in violation of the First Amendment. He also said the move came “completely out of the blue.”

The attorney also pressed the judge to immediately restore the three outlet’s media credentials, nodding to the Chinese leader’s arrival in Washington.

“These are urgent matters,” Boutrous told the judge. “We’re at war. World leaders are coming to Washington.”

Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik contended that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” and that the president has the right to decide who accesses certain spaces.

“At the very least, the president may exclude anyone he wants from the Oval Office,” Velchik later added.

Trump said in advance of the hearing that he expected to lose at the district court level, calling Kelly a “not particularly fair judge.” He indicated he would quickly appeal.

DIESEL DIVIDE DEEPENDS: A divide is emerging in the GOP over how best to respond to rising diesel prices, amid growing calls for lawmakers to consider a ban on exports.

After telling reporters Tuesday that talks within the administration are ongoing about a potential diesel export ban, the White House is now denying a Politico report that says the administration is planning a 90-day ban on exports. Politico, citing five people familiar, reported that the administration was still working out a legal process for such a move.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright told The Wall Street Journal that the administration would not halt all diesel exports and would instead take a voluntary approach to bringing prices down. Wright also was quoted in Reuters yesterday criticizing the ban, saying it “definitely doesn’t work.”

The White House referred The Hill to his comments, when asked about the Politico report.

Still, enthusiasm for a diesel export ban is strong among some constituents. Rep. Ashley Hinson , the Iowa GOP Senate candidate, responded to Trump’s support for a diesel export ban Tuesday by suggesting that Congress return to Washington to make that happen immediately.

“He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying,” Pezeshkian told the room of Trump.

“We will never bow our head or bend at the knee,” he added.

The U.S. representative walked out of the room during the Iranian president’s address.

The speech was at times a direct response to Trump’s remarks on Tuesday, in which he said Iran it has a choice between making a deal with the U.S. or risking “annihilation.”

The Supreme Court has already twice rejected the implementation of a map that would likely increase the state GOP’s edge in its congressional delegation from 6-2 to 7-1. But those rulings have been interim, and a federal appeals court reinstated the 7-1 map on Monday in its final ruling on the case.

That now sends the case back to the high court, but the victory for Republicans may only be temporary.

Given the Supreme Court’s past two rulings against the 7-1 map, a shift to rule in its favor would be a striking turnaround. And with ballots already being sent out in Missouri, time for further debate has essentially run out.

BLUE SHIFT : Democrats’ map in the upcoming midterms keeps expanding as multiple election forecasters shift their analyses of key races in favor of the party’s candidates.

The election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted two Senate races considered reaches for Democrats in their favor Wednesday, moving the South Carolina Senate race from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” and the Kansas Senate race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.”

Both GOP Sens. Roger Marshall (Kan.) and Darline Graham (S.C.) are still viewed as favorites to hold onto their seats, but Democrats are increasingly hopeful they could pull off upsets as polls show a tightening race.

The changes came a day after fellow forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved three Senate races and four gubernatorial races in favor of Democrats , reflecting the “persistently poor national environment” for Republicans.

The Kansas Senate race was one of the three, along with Iowa and Michigan. Sabato’s also moved three key House races toward Democrats, including one new district in Texas that was drawn specifically for the purpose of helping Republicans gain a seat.

Democrats will need to net four seats in November to win back a majority in the Senate, but what at one point seemed to be a stretch now appears possible.

The changes come as the president’s job performance numbers sink to their lowest levels ever recorded from either of his terms, as the cost of gas soars amid an unpopular Iran war. Angela Paxton has largely stayed quiet during the attorney general’s closely watched Senate race against his Democratic opponent, Texas state Rep. James Talarico . Ahead of the primary in May, the state senator encouraged the public to vote but notably did not mention Ken Paxton’s race.

articles.body:
Runs came in waves on Wednesday night in the annual Congressional Women’s Softball Game, with the press corps’s team Bad News Babes besting Team Congress 22-16 at Audi Field.

The 18th annual event saw the nation’s legislators — led by captains Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.V.) and Reps. Julia Fedorchak (R-N.D.) and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.) — face the congressional press corps, led by captains Emily Goodin of the New York Post and Katie Lobosco of Tax Notes. The event raised $882,596 for Youth Survival Coalition (YSC), an organization dedicated to helping young adults diagnosed with breast cancer.

“It’s about raising money for cancer, building some collegiality and making sure that folks feel that there’s some joy in this hard work,” Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.) said of the game before the first pitch.

The game was established in 2009 by a group of lawmakers, including Wasserman Schultz, who had just announced her own battle with breast cancer. The game has raised over $5.8 million for YSC since its founding.

The air was crisp and the lights were bright as players took the field to raucous applause from the crowd at D.C.’s repurposed pro soccer stadium. The Bad News Babes quickly went up 2-1 by the second inning, but Team Congress fought back with key offensive and defensive plays by Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds (R-Northern Mariana Islands).

By the fourth inning, Team Congress had evened the score at 7-7 with key runs batted in by King-Hinds and Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kan.). The scoreboard kept climbing into the fifth with a series of walks by pitcher Rep. Kathy Castor (R-Fla.) that put the press in the lead 14-7.

Castor kept walking batters and the press kept crossing home plate as the press took a 20-10 in the sixth inning.

A home run from Davids in the final inning was a highlight for the Team Congress, but was not enough to surpass America’s First Amendment fighters on the Bad News Babes, who came back from last year’s loss to handily win in the highest-scoring Congressional Women’s Softball Game of all time.

Not far from mind for both sides was President Trump’s ban on three media outlets from the press pool. Hours after the game wrapped up, a district court judge ordered the White House to restore access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

Before the game, Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.) said there is a friendly rivalry, with what she said congresspeople jokingly call their “common enemy.” She said she’d like to see both sides stand up for the free press, calling the White House ban “disgusting.”

“So being here, a friendly game will show that we can work together as Democrats and Republicans,” Craig said. “But I’d also kind of like to see us work together to support a free press in this country.”

Still, the Minnesota Democrat did not mince words when it came to the night’s competition.

“I support their First Amendment right, but I definitely support kicking their ass on the softball field,” Craig said.

Randall said during practices for the annual game, members are able to build relationships with teammates across the aisle. Randall said she has co-sponsored amendments with Fedorchak that stemmed from conversations on the diamond.

Randall said when she was campaigning for her seat in Congress, members including Wasserman Schultz encouraged her to play in the softball game. She said as the first LGBTQ Latina in Congress, she had some “stereotypes to live up to, queer women in sports.”

“I haven’t played softball since junior high, but it’s fun and we have a great team,” Randall said.

Frank Thorp, a coach for the Bad News Babes and a coordinating producer and off-air reporter for NBC News, said he first got involved in the annual game over a decade ago when the press team needed a fill-in coach. He said it has become one of the most impactful things he’s been a part of while covering Capitol Hill.

“I love being a part of it, it’s for a good cause, but it’s also a situation where I’ve gotten to meet so many amazing women, all these amazing journalists that I look up to,” Thorp said. “I’ve got to know them in this really special way and they’re all just a bunch of badasses.”

articles.title: Federal appeals court deals blow to Trump deportation agenda
articles.summary: The First Circuit formally struck down President Donald Trump's third-party country deportation policy after ICE attempted to remove a Peruvian migrant to Ghana this week.
articles.body: A federal appeals court formally struck down the Trump administration's current format for deporting illegal immigrants to third-party countries on Tuesday. The Court of Appeals for the First Circuit issued a ruling last week that endorsed a lower court order that Immigration and Customs Enforcement must allow migrants a meaningful chance to claim they would be endangered if deported to a third-party country. This week, however, ICE officials attempted to move forward with deporting at least one migrant, who originally hails from Peru, to Ghana. LIBERIA AGREES TO ACCEPT 1,200 THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTEES FROM US WITHIN A YEAR The Trump administration has repeatedly used third-party countries for deportations to execute removal orders on migrants who claim they would be tortured if returned to their country of origin. ICE argued the Peruvian migrant, identified as John Doe, could still be removed because the First Circuit had not formally issued a mandate striking down the policy, according to The American Prospect. TRUMP PLANS TO DEPORT IRANIANS TO VIOLENCE-PLAGUED CENTRAL AFRICAN NATION IN NEW DEAL When asked for a clarification this week, the First Circuit formally issued that mandate, striking down a stay that had allowed third-party deportations to continue while the case was being litigated in higher courts. "Consistent with this court's September 18, 2026, Judgment, the March 16, 2026, stay pending appeal is dissolved," the appeals court wrote in a brief order on Wednesday. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT The First Circuit's ruling upheld a February 2026 decision from Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, who contended that the third-party deportations violated migrants' due process rights because it could send them to unfamiliar or dangerous countries without their knowledge. First Circuit Judge Seth Aframe, one of two Biden appointees on a three-judge panel that handed down last week's ruling, argued that Murphy was "sensible" to require DHS to allow migrants a "meaningful" chance to raise concerns about a country to which they could be deported..
